newsitem.title: UK: Business slow in European minor metals.
newsitem.headline: Business slow in European minor metals.

text.p: Trading in industrial minor metals remained largely subdued this week against the backdrop of an industry conference in Miami which was being attended by many market-makers.
The handful of European traders that remained at their desks said business had turned extremely slow, though prices were mainly steady.

Indium probed higher, while cobalt showed further signs of an upside recovery. Antimony managed to hold just above $2,100 a tonne, though one trader suggested small pockets of business had been concluded below this level.

Despite talk that the recent sharp gains in indium had slowed several European traders said business in fairly good volume was seen at above $300 as kilo. Japanese demand against the backdrop of low producer stocks continued to drive the price higher.
"Demand is still brisk and levels of around $310 a kilo have been paid," one trader commented.
He suggested that prices would move higher near-term, possibly towards $400 a kilo.
Consumer enquiry and light bouts of short-covering saw cobalt claw higher, though most traders agreed the market (supply/demand) at present remained well balanced.
Several said prices had bottomed out after recent downside pressure but were unsure if they had the potential to move significantly higher.
Russian material was reported as high as $19.40 a Ib.
High grade was around $20.50 with the backdrop of worn-torn Zaire still only adding background support.
Apart from the unconfirmed report of business below $2,100 antimony traded roughly between $2,125 and $2,150 a tonne in slow volume.
Traders said overall the market was showing a reluctance to break significantly below $2,100.
"There is some nervousness that prices may slip but overall the market is likely to trade in a corridor of between $2,000/$2,100 and $2,400/$2,500 over the foreseeable future," a trader said.
The threat of sales of stockpiled Russian material continued to lose its influence over the minor metals market.
Traders believed between 500 and 2,000 tonnes of chrome could be sold from the strategic stockpiles, but swiftly added, "We will believe it when we see it."
Magnesium was little changed but traders noted that good quality and clean Chinese metal was lacking in Rotterdam warehouses.
Elsewhere, conditions remained stolid amid the lack of trader and consumer participation.
